Baby & Child

Breast development: soreness, uneven growth and changes to check

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A tender breast bud or one side growing before the other can feel surprising. Many breast changes are part of development, but reassurance is most useful when it also explains what to watch for. Breasts continue to respond to hormones and life stages well beyond puberty.

Breast changes begin before puberty and continue through life

The earliest breast structures form before birth, including the nipples and the beginnings of the duct system. The more visible growth of puberty is one stage in a much longer process. Menstrual cycles, pregnancy, lactation, medicines, ageing and menopause can all bring later changes.

There is no birthday when breasts must reach a particular size, and menopause does not mean they can never change again. Understanding the usual pattern can make a new sensation less alarming, but a general explanation of hormones should not be used to dismiss a persistent or unusual symptom.

What a breast bud can feel like

For many girls, the first visible sign of puberty is a small breast bud beneath the nipple and areola, the surrounding darker skin. It may feel like a firm or rubbery disc and can be tender. One side may begin before the other, which can make a normal early change look like a single lump.

Puberty commonly begins between ages 8 and 13. Discuss breast development before age 8, or no development by age 13, with a clinician rather than deciding from appearance alone that something is wrong. If you are unsure whether a lump is a breast bud, an examination can help. Repeatedly squeezing or pressing it is not a useful way to check.

How tissue develops during puberty

As hormone signals change, ducts grow, glandular tissue develops and fat contributes to the breast’s size and shape. Oestrogen and progesterone have different roles within this process. Ducts do not simply turn into glands on the day ovulation starts, and the stages cannot be dated precisely from a photograph or cup size.

The areola and nipple can also change in size or prominence. Development usually unfolds over several years rather than evenly from month to month. A first period often arrives a few years after budding begins, but its timing does not set a final breast size. Comparing classmates can create worry without providing useful medical information.

Why growing breasts can feel sore

Tenderness can accompany developing breast tissue. Later, hormonal changes during a menstrual cycle may produce heaviness, swelling or an ache, often in both breasts. Some people notice more discomfort before a period and improvement once it starts or finishes.

Soreness is not a measure of how much a breast is growing. Itching may come from skin irritation, and back or shoulder pain may have musculoskeletal causes. These symptoms do not prove that puberty is progressing normally. Persistent pain, a focal sore area, a rash or discomfort that affects daily activities deserves advice, especially if it is getting worse.

Uneven growth is common, but new changes still matter

The breasts do not have to develop at the same pace or end up identical. A difference may become less noticeable as development continues, and some asymmetry can remain in adulthood. You do not need to make the two sides match in order to be healthy.

However, rapid enlargement on one side, a new distinct lump, skin changes or a marked change from your usual appearance should be assessed. An unusually large difference that affects comfort or causes distress can also be discussed. Reassurance should address the actual concern rather than insist that every size difference is automatically harmless.

A bra is an option for comfort and support

A soft, well-fitting bra or crop top may reduce rubbing or movement if that feels helpful. A supportive sports bra can be useful during activity. There is no requirement to begin wearing one at a particular age or developmental stage, and it is reasonable to try different styles.

Choose a fit that does not dig in, leave persistent pressure marks or make breathing or movement uncomfortable. A bra does not control final breast size or guarantee protection from every sports injury. If pain persists despite a comfortable fit, speak with a clinician rather than repeatedly buying firmer support.

Lumps should be assessed without assuming the worst

Many breast lumps are benign, meaning non-cancerous. A fluid-filled cyst or a fibroadenoma, a growth of breast tissue, may be responsible. That cannot be established safely from an online description or by deciding whether a lump moves. A new or growing lump should be examined, even when it is painless.

The clinician will consider age, the location, the timing and other symptoms, and may arrange imaging or further tests. Some lumps need observation; others need treatment. A cyst may sometimes be drained or a lesion removed after assessment, but finding a lump does not automatically mean surgery. Do not try to squeeze, drain or massage it away yourself.

Use breast awareness rather than a compulsory monthly ritual

It helps to know how your breasts usually look and feel so that a new change can be described. That is different from teaching every child a formal monthly cancer self-examination from the start of puberty. Routine self-examination has not shown a clear benefit as a screening programme and can lead to unnecessary investigations.

Awareness does not require repeatedly checking for tiny differences throughout the day. Report a concerning change rather than waiting for a scheduled self-check or screening appointment. Later screening decisions depend on age, risk and local guidance; neither a home examination nor a recent normal screening result replaces assessment of a new symptom.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding bring another set of changes

During pregnancy, breasts may become fuller and tender as the tissue prepares for milk production. The areolas can become larger and darker, veins may be more visible and nipples may tingle or feel sore. These changes vary; their absence or intensity does not by itself establish whether a pregnancy is healthy.

The breast continues to respond during milk production and after breastfeeding ends. A new painful red area, a persistent lump or feeling feverish should not simply be written off as expected enlargement. Ask for appropriate maternity or breastfeeding support if there is a new problem. Breast size alone does not determine someone’s worth or success as a parent.

Perimenopause and menopause do not stop all breast change

As ovarian hormone levels change around menopause, breast tissue, fullness and firmness may change too. The timing varies and is not fixed at age 50. Weight changes and skin elasticity can also affect the outline, so there is no single shape that everyone should expect.

Hormone therapy can cause soreness or swelling in some people. Discuss troublesome effects with the prescriber rather than changing the dose yourself. A new lump, discharge or a one-sided change after menopause still needs assessment; it should not be assumed to be an ordinary result of ageing.

Breast growth during feminising hormone treatment

Feminising hormone therapy can also lead to breast budding, tenderness and uneven early growth. The amount and pace of development vary, and changes can take years. A particular cup size cannot be promised from a medicine dose or another person’s results.

Taking extra oestrogen does not reliably make development faster or larger and may increase harm. Work with the prescribing clinician on goals, side effects and monitoring. A new breast symptom still deserves assessment during hormone treatment, just as it does at other stages of life. Do not assume that every lump or discharge is explained by the prescription.

Nipple and skin changes that need attention

Contact a clinician about unexplained nipple discharge, especially if it is bloody, pus-like, spontaneous or comes from one side. Milky fluid can be expected with breastfeeding, but milk-like discharge outside that context may also need investigation. Its colour alone cannot identify the cause.

New nipple pulling-in, persistent nipple pain or redness, dimpling, thickened skin, swelling or an unexplained change in shape should also be checked. A nipple that has always been inverted is different from one that has newly changed. A red, hot, painful breast with fever or feeling unwell needs prompt care. These signs have several possible causes; seeking help is sensible, not a prediction of cancer.

Make it easy to ask for help

If you are supporting a young person, use clear anatomical words, respect their privacy and avoid commenting on whether their development is early, late or attractive. Offer practical help with a comfortable garment or an appointment without turning the change into a family discussion they did not choose.

At a visit, explain when the change started, whether it follows the menstrual cycle and whether there is a lump, discharge, rash or fever. Bring a medicine list, including hormones and supplements. You can ask what examination or test is being proposed and why. A clinician can also help distinguish ordinary development from a problem that needs follow-up.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pubertal budding, tenderness and asymmetry are common; timing and new symptoms should be assessed individually.

Breast awareness differs from routine cancer self-examination, and unexplained discharge or a new lump should not be dismissed as hormonal.

How BeMama can help

Note the timing and the specific change, then ask for help if it persists or concerns you. Respect a young person’s privacy during that conversation.

When to seek help

Paediatric, breast-health and hormone-care review remain pending. This is developmental education, not a diagnosis or screening schedule.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Development occurs at different rates and can start on one side.
  • Soreness does not measure growth, and a bra is a comfort choice.
  • A new lump or nipple change deserves assessment.
  • Breasts can change during pregnancy, menopause and prescribed hormone treatment.

Frequently asked questions

What does a breast bud feel like?

It may feel like a small firm or rubbery disc under the nipple and areola, sometimes with tenderness. Ask for an assessment if you are unsure.

When should I ask about the timing of puberty?

Discuss development before age 8 or no breast development by age 13 with a clinician. These are reasons for review, not a diagnosis by themselves.

Is one side growing first always a problem?

No. It is common, but a new distinct lump, rapid enlargement, significant discomfort or skin changes needs assessment.

Does more pain mean more growth?

No. Pain is not a measure of breast growth and can have causes unrelated to development.

Do I have to wear a bra as soon as budding starts?

No. Choose support if it feels comfortable or helps during activity; there is no mandatory starting age.

Does every breast lump need surgery?

No. Treatment depends on the cause. Some need observation, but a clinician should assess a new lump first.

Should children start monthly cancer self-exams at puberty?

A compulsory monthly screening ritual is not recommended here. Understanding usual appearance and reporting a new change is more useful.

Is milk-coloured nipple discharge always normal?

No. It can be expected during breastfeeding, but unexplained discharge outside that context should be checked.

Can extra oestrogen speed up breast growth?

It does not reliably improve the result and may increase risk. Follow the prescribing clinician’s plan.

Can breasts still change after menopause?

Yes. Hormones, medicines, weight and ageing can affect them. A new lump or unusual one-sided change still needs assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
